q: The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution make up this document. It protects freedoms of speech, religion, and the press. James Madison drafted it. For 10 points, name this set of amendments.

Abraham Lincoln delivered this very short speech at a Pennsylvania battlefield in November 1863. It begins "Four score and seven years ago." It ends with a "government of the people, by the people, for the people." For 10 points, name this speech.

People in many countries use this system of units, based on tens, that includes the liter, meter, and gram. It was developed in France during the Revolution. The United States uses a different customary system. For 10 points, name this system.

On this temperature scale, water freezes at thirty-two degrees and boils at two hundred twelve degrees at sea level. It is named for a German physicist who also invented the mercury thermometer. The United States uses it for weather reports. For 10 points, name this scale.

This kind of triangle has three sides of equal length and three angles of sixty degrees. Its name comes from Latin roots meaning "equal sides." Every equiangular triangle is also one of these. For 10 points, name this triangle.

This instrument measures atmospheric pressure and was invented by Evangelista Torricelli. Its name comes from Greek words for "weight" and "measure." Falling readings often predict a storm. For 10 points, name this weather instrument.
This device with a gnomon casts a shadow to tell time. Ancient Egyptians and Greeks used it. It cannot work at night or on cloudy days. For 10 points, name this timekeeping device.

This tool with a flat scale of inches or centimeters is used to measure and draw straight lines. Students keep one in a pencil case. Wooden, plastic, and metal ones are common, and a longer version is a yardstick. For 10 points, name this tool.

This instrument with a needle and a circular scale of degrees measures the angle of a line or arc. Students use it in geometry class. It is usually semicircular and made of clear plastic. For 10 points, name this tool.

This English word names a book of maps. Its name comes from a Titan of Greek myth who held up the sky. Gerardus Mercator popularized the name in the sixteenth century. For 10 points, name this reference book.
Answer these questions about units of measurement.
parts: How many inches are in one foot?
Which unit of volume in the United States is divided into four quarts?
What unit measures the distance light travels in a year?

q: Answer these questions about languages.
parts: What is the most widely spoken first language in China?
Which language is the official language of Brazil?
Which language is written with the Devanagari script and is widely spoken in India?

parts: What word describes a word with the same sound as another but a different meaning, such as "two" and "too"?
What part of speech names a person, place, or thing?
What name is given to a word formed from the first letters of other words, such as NASA?

q: Answer these questions about important documents.
parts: Which document sets up the government of the United States and begins "We the People"?
Which document, issued on January 1, 1863, declared enslaved people in the Confederate states to be free?
Which French document of 1789 stated that men are born and remain free and equal in rights?

q: Answer these questions about numbers and counting.
parts: What is the name for a number divisible only by one and itself, such as 7?
What system of numbers uses only the digits zero and one?
What term describes a number multiplied by itself, such as 25 from 5?

q: Answer these questions about libraries and books.
parts: What term describes a book about a real person's life written by someone else?
What term describes a book of fiction that is typically a long story with chapters?
What term describes the list at the back of a book that names topics and their page numbers?

q: Answer these questions about maps and directions.
parts: On most maps, which compass direction is toward the top of the page?
What name is given to imaginary east-west lines that measure distance from the equator?
What name is given to the explanatory box on a map that explains its symbols?

q: In December 1773, colonists disguised as Mohawk Indians boarded three ships in a Massachusetts harbor. They dumped 342 chests of a taxed product overboard to protest the Tea Act. Parliament answered with the Coercive Acts, which the colonists called the Intolerable Acts. For 10 points, name this protest that took place in Boston.

This man was the principal author of a 1776 document that begins by asserting that all men are created equal. He later served as the third president of the United States. He lived at a Virginia estate called Monticello. For 10 points, name this author of the Declaration of Independence.

In 1803, Robert Livingston and James Monroe negotiated this deal with France. Napoleon sold roughly 828,000 square miles of land to the United States for 15 million dollars. It doubled the size of the young country and gave it control of the port of New Orleans. For 10 points, name this land purchase named for a territory west of the Mississippi River.

A young Shoshone woman named Sacagawea served as interpreter and guide on this journey. Thomas Jefferson ordered it to explore the lands west of the Mississippi River and find a water route to the Pacific. It was led by two men who set out from near Saint Louis in 1804. For 10 points, name this expedition led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark.

This speech begins with the words "Four score and seven years ago." It was delivered in November 1863 at the dedication of a cemetery for soldiers who died in a Pennsylvania battle. It ends by calling for a "new birth of freedom." For 10 points, name this short speech by Abraham Lincoln.

This woman escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and then returned to the South about thirteen times to guide others to freedom. She worked as a conductor on a network of safe houses and secret routes. She was nicknamed "Moses" by those she helped. For 10 points, name this abolitionist and conductor on the Underground Railroad.

Issued on January 1, 1863, this order declared that slaves in states in rebellion against the Union were free. It did not apply to the border states that stayed loyal to the Union. It changed the aims of the Civil War by making the end of slavery a goal of the Union. For 10 points, name this proclamation of Abraham Lincoln.

The Central Pacific and Union Pacific companies built this project from opposite directions. Chinese and Irish immigrants did much of the backbreaking labor. Its two lines were joined by a ceremonial golden spike at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869. For 10 points, name this rail line that connected the eastern and western halves of the United States.

On the morning of December 7, 1941, Japanese planes bombed American warships in Hawaii. Eight battleships were damaged or sunk, and more than 2,400 Americans were killed. The next day, Franklin Roosevelt called the date "a day that will live in infamy." For 10 points, name this attack that brought the United States into World War II.

In December 1955, this seamstress refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery, Alabama. Her arrest led to a boycott that lasted more than a year and made a young minister into a leader. She is often called the "mother of the civil rights movement." For 10 points, name this woman.

This man led the 1963 March on Washington, where he gave his "I Have a Dream" speech on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. He earned the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 for his use of nonviolent protest. He was assassinated in Memphis in 1968. For 10 points, name this Baptist minister and civil rights leader.

This president led the country through the Great Depression and most of World War II. He was elected four times and used radio "fireside chats" to speak directly to the public. His New Deal created programs such as Social Security and the Civilian Conservation Corps. For 10 points, name this president who served from 1933 to 1945.

This economic crisis began after the stock market crash of October 1929. Banks failed, factories closed, and about a quarter of American workers lost their jobs at its worst point. Soup kitchens and shantytowns known as Hoovervilles appeared in many cities. For 10 points, name this decade-long downturn that preceded the New Deal.

In the 1830s, the Cherokee and other southeastern tribes were forced to move to land west of the Mississippi River. Andrew Jackson had signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830. Thousands of Cherokee died of disease, cold, and hunger on the march to present-day Oklahoma. For 10 points, name this forced relocation whose name refers to weeping.

In 1848, James Marshall found shiny flakes in the American River at Sutter's Mill. News of the discovery drew about 300,000 people to California, many of them called forty-niners. San Francisco grew from a small village into a large city. For 10 points, name this rush that began in 1848.

In 1620, a group of English Separatists crossed the Atlantic on this ship and landed at Plymouth, Massachusetts. Before going ashore, 41 men signed a compact to govern themselves. For 10 points, name this ship that carried the Pilgrims to America.

The Virginia Company of London founded this colony in 1607 on a river named for the king. John Smith helped it survive a "starving time" by enforcing the rule that men who did not work did not eat. John Rolfe's tobacco later made the colony profitable. For 10 points, name this first permanent English settlement in North America.

James Madison proposed these amendments in 1789 to win over critics who feared a strong national government. Ratified in 1791, they protect freedoms of speech, religion, and the press. They also guarantee the right to a jury trial. For 10 points, name these first ten amendments to the Constitution.

This Philadelphia printer published Poor Richard's Almanack. He conducted a famous experiment with a kite and a key during a storm and invented bifocals. He also helped draft the Declaration of Independence and appears on the hundred-dollar bill. For 10 points, name this American statesman and inventor.

This man was the first Secretary of the Treasury under George Washington. He wrote most of the Federalist Papers with James Madison and John Jay and created the First Bank of the United States. He died in a duel with Aaron Burr in 1804. For 10 points, name this man who appears on the ten-dollar bill.

Completed in 1825 under Governor DeWitt Clinton, this man-made waterway linked the Hudson River to Lake Erie. It lowered shipping costs and helped turn New York City into the nation's leading port. Critics had mocked it as "Clinton's Ditch." For 10 points, name this canal in New York State.

In 1793, this inventor patented a machine that quickly separated seeds from short-staple cotton. It made cotton farming far more profitable and increased the demand for enslaved labor in the South. He also promoted the idea of interchangeable parts for muskets. For 10 points, name this American inventor of the cotton gin.

In December 1903, two brothers from Dayton, Ohio, made the first powered, controlled airplane flights near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. The longest of their first four flights that day lasted 59 seconds. Their plane was named the Flyer. For 10 points, name these two brothers, Orville and Wilbur.

Born into slavery in Maryland, this man taught himself to read and escaped to the North in 1838. He published an autobiography called Narrative of the Life and wrote for his newspaper The North Star. He later advised Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this great abolitionist orator.

Beginning in the early 1930s, drought and poor farming practices turned the Great Plains into this disaster zone. Huge dust storms swept across Oklahoma, Kansas, and Texas and forced many families to flee to California. John Steinbeck described this migration in The Grapes of Wrath. For 10 points, name this environmental disaster of the 1930s.

In October 1962, American spy planes photographed Soviet missile sites under construction on an island in the Caribbean. President John F. Kennedy ordered a naval blockade, which he called a quarantine. After tense days, Nikita Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. For 10 points, name this Cold War confrontation over Cuba.

This president led the Rough Riders up San Juan Hill in the Spanish-American War. As president, he broke up trusts, created national parks, and began building the Panama Canal. His motto was to "speak softly and carry a big stick." For 10 points, name this man who served from 1901 to 1909.

In October 1781, General Charles Cornwallis surrendered his army to George Washington at this Virginia town. French ships blocked the British escape by sea while French and American soldiers surrounded the town on land. The surrender effectively ended major fighting in the American Revolution. For 10 points, name this battle.

Passed in 1820, this law admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state. It also banned slavery in the Louisiana Territory north of the 36 degrees 30 minutes line. Henry Clay helped broker it to preserve the balance in the Senate. For 10 points, name this agreement.

Issued in 1823, this policy was announced in a message to Congress by a president from Virginia. It warned European powers not to colonize or interfere in the Western Hemisphere. In return, the United States promised to stay out of European affairs. For 10 points, name this foreign policy statement named for James Monroe.

In 1803, Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the opinion in this case, which arose when William Marbury did not receive his commission as a justice of the peace. The Court ruled that part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional. This established the power of judicial review. For 10 points, name this case.

In 1857, the Supreme Court ruled in this case that African Americans could not be citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote the opinion. It outraged northerners and helped push the nation toward civil war. For 10 points, name this case brought by an enslaved man from Missouri.
Answer these questions about the American Revolution.
parts: Which Boston silversmith rode on the night of April 18, 1775, to warn that the British were coming?
The "shot heard round the world" was fired in which pair of Massachusetts towns where the war began?
Which Pennsylvania site was where George Washington's army spent the winter of 1777 to 1778 and trained under Baron von Steuben?

parts: Which Union general led the Army of the Potomac's final campaign and later became president?

parts: Which 1787 gathering in Philadelphia wrote the United States Constitution?
Which 1812 conflict with Great Britain saw the burning of Washington, D.C., and inspired the Star-Spangled Banner?
Which president, known as Old Hickory, was nominated by the Democratic Party and fought the Second Bank of the United States?

q: In June 1215, English barons forced King John to put his seal on this document at Runnymede. It said that the king was subject to the law and promised that free men could not be punished except by lawful judgment. Its name is Latin for "Great Charter." For 10 points, name this document that limited royal power in England.

This English king broke with the Roman Catholic Church in the 1530s so that he could end his marriage to Catherine of Aragon. Parliament made him head of the Church of England through the Act of Supremacy. He married six times, including Anne Boleyn and Jane Seymour. For 10 points, name this Tudor king.

This daughter of Anne Boleyn became queen in 1558 and ruled for 44 years. Her reign saw the defeat of a Spanish fleet and the plays of William Shakespeare. She never married and was called the Virgin Queen. For 10 points, name this Tudor monarch.

This Corsican-born general crowned himself emperor of the French in 1804 in Notre-Dame Cathedral. He won victories across Europe and then lost most of his army in a disastrous winter retreat from Moscow. His legal reforms are known as the Civil Code. For 10 points, name this French ruler.

In July 1789, a Paris crowd stormed this fortress and prison, which symbolized royal tyranny. Its fall is celebrated in France every July 14. The event is usually seen as the start of the French Revolution. For 10 points, name this fortress.

This king of France ruled for 72 years, from 1643 to 1715. He called himself the Sun King and built an enormous palace outside Paris that became the center of his court. He fought several expensive wars to expand French power. For 10 points, name this monarch.

This disease reached Europe in 1347 on trading ships from the Black Sea. Carried by fleas on rats, it killed a huge share of the continent's population over the next few years. Its victims developed painful swellings called buboes. For 10 points, name this medieval plague.

This "rebirth" of art and learning began in the Italian city-states in the 1300s. Wealthy patrons such as the Medici family paid artists to create new works. Thinkers called humanists studied the writings of ancient Greece and Rome. For 10 points, name this period of European history that produced Michelangelo and Raphael.

This painter and inventor filled thousands of pages of notebooks with drawings of flying machines and human anatomy. He painted The Last Supper in Milan and a portrait of a woman with a famous smile. He was born in the town of Vinci. For 10 points, name this Italian Renaissance genius who painted the Mona Lisa.

In 1517, a German monk is said to have nailed his Ninety-five Theses to the door of a church in Wittenberg. He attacked the sale of indulgences and taught that people are saved by faith alone. His ideas began the Protestant Reformation. For 10 points, name this German reformer.

Around 1450, a German goldsmith from Mainz developed a way to print with movable metal type. His most famous product was a Latin Bible. The invention made books cheaper and helped spread ideas across Europe. For 10 points, name this man, the inventor of the European printing press.

In 1588, King Philip II of Spain sent about 130 ships under the Duke of Medina Sidonia to invade England. English fire ships scattered the fleet at Calais, and storms wrecked many of the survivors on the way home. The defeat was a triumph for Elizabeth I. For 10 points, name this failed invasion fleet.

On June 18, 1815, a French army was defeated in a battle in present-day Belgium. The Duke of Wellington held the line until Prussian troops under Gebhard von Blucher arrived. Napoleon was exiled again after this loss. For 10 points, name this battle.

This revolution began in Great Britain in the late 1700s. Inventions such as the spinning jenny and James Watt's improved steam engine moved production from homes to factories. Cities grew rapidly as workers left farms. For 10 points, name this shift to machine-based manufacturing.

This war began in 1914 after the assassination of an Austrian archduke. The Allied Powers, including France, Britain, and Russia, fought the Central Powers, including Germany and Austria-Hungary. Fighting along the Western Front bogged down in trenches. For 10 points, name this conflict that ended in 1918.

On June 28, 1914, this nineteen-year-old Bosnian Serb fired the shots that killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo. He belonged to a group seeking to unite Slavic peoples. Because of his age, he was spared the death penalty and died in prison in 1918. For 10 points, name this assassin whose act set off World War I.

Signed in 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors, this treaty ended World War I with Germany. It required Germany to give up land, limit its army, and accept responsibility for the war. Many Germans bitterly resented its terms. For 10 points, name this treaty named for a French palace.

This man became chancellor of Germany in 1933 and ruled as dictator until 1945. He wrote Mein Kampf while in prison and led the Nazi Party. His invasion of Poland in 1939 started World War II in Europe. For 10 points, name this German leader.

This man became British prime minister in May 1940 and promised the nation "blood, toil, tears and sweat." He led Britain through World War II and gave the "Iron Curtain" speech in 1946. He was also a painter and a Nobel Prize winner in Literature. For 10 points, name this British leader.

In the summer of 1940, the German Luftwaffe tried to win control of the skies over southern England. Radar and the skill of Spitfire and Hurricane pilots helped the Royal Air Force win. Hitler postponed his invasion plans. For 10 points, name this air campaign.

This event was the Nazi regime's systematic murder of about six million Jews and millions of other victims during World War II. Camps such as Auschwitz and Treblinka were built for this purpose. For 10 points, name this genocide.

Sailing in longships, these Scandinavian raiders attacked the monastery of Lindisfarne in 793. They later settled in Iceland, Normandy, and parts of England. Leif Erikson reached North America around the year 1000. For 10 points, name these seafaring people from Norway, Sweden, and Denmark.

This king of the Franks was crowned emperor by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day in the year 800. He ruled much of western Europe and supported scholars at his court in Aachen. His name means "Charles the Great." For 10 points, name this ruler.

In 1066, Duke William of Normandy defeated King Harold Godwinson at this battle on the southeast coast of England. Harold was said to have been killed by an arrow. The Bayeux Tapestry shows scenes from this battle. For 10 points, name this battle that began the Norman conquest of England.

Beginning in 1095, European knights marched to the Middle East after Pope Urban II called for help against Muslim rulers. Their goal was to capture Jerusalem. Later expeditions included the Third, led in part by Richard the Lionheart. For 10 points, name these medieval religious wars.

This French peasant girl said that she heard the voices of saints telling her to drive out the English. She helped lift the siege of Orleans in 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned. She was burned at the stake in Rouen in 1431. For 10 points, name this saint and national heroine of France.

This Russian tsar traveled incognito in western Europe and returned to modernize his country. He founded the city of Saint Petersburg in 1703 and forced nobles to cut their beards. He defeated Sweden in the Great Northern War. For 10 points, name this ruler who ruled from 1682 to 1725.

This German-born empress seized power from her husband in 1762 and ruled Russia for over three decades. She corresponded with Voltaire and expanded Russian territory south to the Black Sea. For 10 points, name this woman, whose title includes the word "Great."

This Bolshevik leader returned to Russia in April 1917 and took power in the October Revolution. He founded the Soviet state and led it through a civil war. His body is on display in a mausoleum in Red Square. For 10 points, name this first leader of the Soviet Union.

As Minister President of Prussia, this man used wars against Denmark, Austria, and France to unify Germany in 1871. He was known as the "Iron Chancellor" and was said to favor "blood and iron." He later created the first social insurance programs. For 10 points, name this German statesman.

This lawyer led the Committee of Public Safety during the French Revolution. He oversaw the Reign of Terror, during which thousands were sent to the guillotine. He was himself guillotined in July 1794. For 10 points, name this Jacobin leader.

In October 1805, a British fleet under Horatio Nelson defeated the combined French and Spanish navies off the coast of Spain. Nelson was shot by a sniper and died during the battle. The victory ended Napoleon's hope of invading Britain. For 10 points, name this naval battle.

These treaties of 1648 ended the Thirty Years' War in the Holy Roman Empire. They recognized the independence of the Dutch Republic and the Swiss Confederation. They are often seen as the start of the modern system of sovereign states. For 10 points, name this peace.

After the defeat of Napoleon, diplomats met in this city from 1814 to 1815 to redraw Europe's map. Klemens von Metternich of Austria was its dominant figure. They sought a balance of power and restored many old ruling families. For 10 points, name this congress.

King Henry IV of France issued this decree in 1598 to give French Protestants known as Huguenots the right to worship in some places. It ended decades of religious wars. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685. For 10 points, name this edict, named for a city in western France.

After King Charles I was executed in 1649, this Puritan military leader ruled England without a king. He had led the New Model Army to victory in the English Civil War. He took the title Lord Protector in 1653. For 10 points, name this man.
Answer these questions about the Tudor monarchs of England.
parts: Which second wife of Henry VIII was executed in 1536 and was the mother of Elizabeth I?
Which daughter of Henry VIII, nicknamed "Bloody Mary," restored Catholicism in England?
Which king won the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485 and founded the Tudor dynasty?

parts: Which style of fighting, in long ditches protected by barbed wire, characterized the Western Front?
Which British ocean liner was sunk by a German submarine in 1915, killing many Americans?
Which 1916 battle in northeastern France was one of the longest of the war and became a symbol of French determination?

parts: Which country was invaded by Germany in September 1939, bringing Britain and France into the war?
From which French beach town were more than 300,000 Allied soldiers evacuated across the English Channel in 1940?
Which Soviet city on the Volga was the site of a turning point battle in 1942 and 1943?

parts: Which artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
Which family of bankers ruled Florence for much of the 1400s and supported artists such as Botticelli?
Which Florentine diplomat wrote The Prince?

parts: Napoleon's army marched into which large country in 1812 and was forced to retreat in winter?
On which Mediterranean island was Napoleon first exiled in 1814?
At which 1805 battle in present-day Czech lands did Napoleon defeat the Russians and Austrians?

q: Answer these questions about medieval Europe.
parts: What kind of fortified stone building did a medieval lord live in?
Which system exchanged land from a lord for loyalty and military service from a vassal?
Which survey, ordered by William the Conqueror in 1085, recorded the landholdings of England?

q: Answer these questions about Russian history.
parts: What title, derived from the Latin Caesar, was held by the rulers of Russia before 1917?
Which family ruled Russia from 1613 until the revolution of 1917?
Who was the last Russian emperor, who abdicated in March 1917?

q: Answer these questions about the French Revolution.
parts: Which king of France was executed by guillotine in January 1793?
Which assembly of representatives of the clergy, nobility, and commoners did the French king call in 1789?
Which pledge, taken on an indoor royal tennis court at Versailles in June 1789, vowed not to disband until France had a constitution?

q: This monument was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE on the west bank of the Nile. It was the tallest human-made structure in the world for thousands of years. It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still largely survives. For 10 points, name this largest pyramid at Giza.

In 49 BCE, this Roman general crossed the Rubicon River with his army and began a civil war. He became dictator for life and reformed the calendar. On the Ides of March in 44 BCE, he was stabbed by senators including Brutus and Cassius. For 10 points, name this Roman leader.

Born Gaius Octavius, this man was the grand-nephew and adopted heir of Julius Caesar. After defeating his rivals, he took a new name in 27 BCE and became Rome's first emperor. His long reign began the Pax Romana. For 10 points, name this ruler.

This woman was the last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt. She allied with Julius Caesar and later with Mark Antony. After her defeat in 31 BCE, she died by suicide, traditionally by the bite of an asp. For 10 points, name this queen of Egypt.

This king of Macedon took the throne at age twenty after his father Philip II was murdered. He defeated the Persian king Darius III at the battle of Gaugamela. He built an empire that reached as far as India before he died in Babylon in 323 BCE. For 10 points, name this conqueror.

This Greek city-state had two kings and a rigid military society. Boys began state training called the agoge at age seven. Its economy depended on enslaved helots who farmed the land. For 10 points, name this rival of Athens, a city in the Peloponnese.

Built in the fifth century BCE on the Acropolis, this temple honored the goddess Athena. The sculptor Phidias oversaw its decoration. Some of its marble sculptures are in the British Museum and are called the Elgin Marbles. For 10 points, name this Greek temple.

This Athenian philosopher taught by asking questions in a method named for him. He was convicted in 399 BCE of corrupting youth and failing to honor the city's gods. He drank poison hemlock rather than flee. For 10 points, name this teacher of Plato.

In about 1754 BCE, this king of Babylon had a collection of laws carved on a stone pillar. Its penalties often followed the principle of "an eye for an eye." The pillar was found in 1901 and now stands in the Louvre. For 10 points, name this ruler whose code is one of the oldest written legal codes.

French soldiers found this inscribed slab near the Nile delta in 1799. It carries the same decree written in hieroglyphs, a cursive Egyptian script, and Greek. Jean-Francois Champollion used it to decipher hieroglyphs. For 10 points, name this stone, now in the British Museum.

Howard Carter discovered the nearly intact tomb of this pharaoh in the Valley of the Kings in 1922. The young ruler took the throne as a boy and died around age eighteen. His golden death mask is world famous. For 10 points, name this "boy king" of Egypt.

Egyptian civilization grew along this river, whose yearly flood left rich black silt on its banks. It flows north through Egypt into the Mediterranean Sea. Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt were named for their positions along it. For 10 points, name this river.

The Sumerians pressed a reed stylus into wet clay to create this early system of writing. Its signs were wedge-shaped. It was used for languages including Akkadian and was eventually written on thousands of clay tablets in Mesopotamia. For 10 points, name this script.

Completed in 80 CE, this huge amphitheater in Rome could seat about fifty thousand spectators. It hosted gladiator fights and staged hunts. Its official name comes from the Flavian dynasty. For 10 points, name this ruined arena.

In 218 BCE, this general from Carthage led an army including war elephants across the Alps into Italy. He crushed the Romans at Cannae in 216 BCE. He was finally beaten at Zama in 202 BCE by Scipio Africanus. For 10 points, name this commander.

The first of these conflicts began over Sicily in 264 BCE. The second featured Hannibal's invasion of Italy. The third ended in 146 BCE with the destruction of Carthage. For 10 points, name these three wars between Rome and Carthage.

In 313, this emperor and Licinius issued the Edict of Milan, which granted tolerance to Christians. He won the Battle of the Milvian Bridge in 312. In 330 he dedicated a new capital on the site of Byzantium. For 10 points, name this emperor for whom that city was named.

In 79 CE, Mount Vesuvius buried this Roman city under volcanic ash. Its streets, shops, and even loaves of bread were preserved. Excavations began in the 1700s and show everyday life in the Roman Empire. For 10 points, name this city near Naples.

In 490 BCE, an Athenian army under Miltiades defeated a Persian invasion force on a plain northeast of Athens. According to legend, a runner carried news of the victory to the city. For 10 points, name this battle that gave its name to a long-distance race.

In 480 BCE, King Leonidas and about 300 Spartans held a narrow mountain pass against the huge army of Xerxes I. A local man named Ephialtes betrayed a path around them. The Greeks fought to the death while other forces retreated. For 10 points, name this battle.

This Athenian statesman led the city during its golden age and delivered a famous funeral oration. He promoted democracy and ordered the construction of the Parthenon. He died in a plague in 429 BCE. For 10 points, name this leader of Athens during its golden age.

In 539 BCE, this man captured Babylon and founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire. A clay cylinder describes his tolerant policies. He allowed exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem. For 10 points, name this Persian king whose title includes the word "Great."

This ruler unified China in 221 BCE and took a new title meaning "first emperor." He standardized writing, money, and weights and measures. He was buried near an army of thousands of life-size clay soldiers. For 10 points, name this founder of the Qin dynasty.

This network of trade routes linked China to the Mediterranean world during the Han dynasty. Caravans carried silk, spices, and paper west and gold and horses east. Ideas such as Buddhism also spread along it. For 10 points, name this system of routes named for a luxury fabric.

Held every four years in honor of Zeus, these athletic contests were traditionally first held in 776 BCE. They took place at a sanctuary in the Peloponnese. A modern revival began in Athens in 1896. For 10 points, name this athletic festival.

These seafaring traders came from cities such as Tyre and Sidon in present-day Lebanon. They were famous for purple dye made from sea snails. Their simple alphabet became the ancestor of the Greek alphabet and our own. For 10 points, name these people who founded Carthage.

Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were major cities of this Bronze Age civilization, which flourished from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. It had planned streets laid out in grids and brick drains. Its script has never been deciphered. For 10 points, name this civilization of present-day Pakistan and India.

The historian Thucydides recorded this conflict, which lasted from 431 to 404 BCE. Pericles led Athens through its early years, and a plague killed thousands. It ended with Athens surrendering to a Spartan-led alliance. For 10 points, name this war between two Greek powers.

This Thracian gladiator escaped from a training school in Capua in 73 BCE and led a major slave rebellion. His army defeated several Roman forces before Marcus Licinius Crassus crushed it. Thousands of captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way. For 10 points, name this rebel leader.

In 31 BCE, Marcus Agrippa commanded the fleet of Octavian at this naval battle off the western coast of Greece. It defeated the forces of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. Octavian soon became the sole ruler of Rome. For 10 points, name this battle.

This emperor reigned from 284 to 305 and divided the empire's administration among four rulers in a system called the Tetrarchy. He launched the last great persecution of Christians. Unusually, he retired voluntarily to a palace on the Adriatic. For 10 points, name this Roman emperor.

This Byzantine emperor ordered a collection of Roman law that became the foundation of many European legal systems. He rebuilt the Hagia Sophia after the Nika riots and his generals, including Belisarius, reconquered parts of Italy and North Africa. His wife was Theodora. For 10 points, name this emperor.

Created around 450 BCE, this first written code of Roman law was posted publicly so that plebeians could know their rights. It was carved on bronze or wooden tablets and covered topics such as debt and family law. For 10 points, name this set of laws named for the number of tablets.

parts: Which Egyptian monument, a lion with a human head, sits near the Great Pyramid?
What process of preserving a dead body with natron and linen wrappings did the Egyptians practice?
Which pharaoh of the nineteenth dynasty built the temples at Abu Simbel and reigned for about sixty-six years?

parts: Which two rivers gave Mesopotamia its name, meaning "land between the rivers"?
Which stepped temple tower dominated many Mesopotamian cities?
Which Babylonian king, reigning from 605 to 562 BCE, is traditionally credited with building the Hanging Gardens?

parts: Which emperor is said to have played music while Rome burned in 64 CE?
Which emperor ordered a defensive wall built across northern Britain around 122 CE?
Which philosopher-emperor, who died in 180, wrote the Meditations?

parts: Which philosopher wrote the Republic and founded the Academy in Athens?
Which philosopher, a student of the Academy founder, tutored Alexander the Great and founded the Lyceum?
Which philosopher from Samos is credited with a famous theorem about right triangles and taught that numbers underlie reality?

q: Answer these questions about government in classical Athens.
parts: What word, from Greek roots meaning "rule by the people," describes the system pioneered in Athens?
What alliance of Greek city-states, led by Athens, was formed in 478 BCE and had its treasury on the island of Delos?
What practice let Athenians vote to exile a citizen for ten years by writing his name on pottery shards?

q: Answer these questions about ancient Greek writers.
parts: Which poet is credited with composing the Iliad and the Odyssey?
Which historian, called the "Father of History," wrote about the Persian Wars?
Which playwright wrote Oedipus Rex and Antigone?

q: Answer these questions about daily life in ancient Rome.
parts: Which language did the Romans speak?
What was the central public square of Rome, where people met for politics and business?
What name is given to the roughly two centuries of peace and prosperity that began under Augustus?

Which dynasty, which lasted about four hundred years, followed the Qin and opened the Silk Road?
Which Chinese historian wrote the Records of the Grand Historian under the dynasty that followed the Qin?

Which king, murdered in 336 BCE, was the father of Alexander?
What was the name of Alexander's famous horse?

q: Born with the name Temujin, this leader united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and took a new title meaning "universal ruler." His cavalry conquered much of Central Asia and northern China. His descendants went on to build the largest contiguous land empire in history. For 10 points, name this Mongol leader who died in 1227.

This grandson of Genghis Khan completed the conquest of China and founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271. The Venetian traveler Marco Polo claimed to have served at his court. His attempts to invade Japan failed when storms destroyed his fleets. For 10 points, name this Mongol emperor.

This ruler of the Mali Empire made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 and gave away so much gold that its price fell in Cairo. His reign made the city of Timbuktu a center of learning. For 10 points, name this wealthy West African king.

The Shona people built this large stone-walled city in southern Africa between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. Its Great Enclosure has granite walls that were built without mortar. It gave its name to a modern country. For 10 points, name this archaeological site.

This island city in Lake Texcoco was the capital of the Aztec Empire. Causeways connected it to the mainland. After its fall in 1521 to Spanish forces, Mexico City was built on its ruins. For 10 points, name this city.

In 1519, this Spanish conquistador landed in Mexico with about 500 men. With help from native allies such as the Tlaxcalans, he captured the Aztec capital and the emperor Montezuma. For 10 points, name this explorer who conquered the Aztec Empire.

Machu Picchu was built in the Andes mountains by this empire, whose capital was Cusco. Its people kept records with knotted strings called quipus and built a vast network of roads. Francisco Pizarro captured its ruler Atahualpa in 1532. For 10 points, name this South American empire.

This Mesoamerican civilization built stepped pyramids at Chichen Itza and Tikal. Its scribes wrote in a system of glyphs and kept a complex calendar. The great cities of its Classic period in the southern lowlands declined around 900. For 10 points, name this civilization of the Yucatan and Guatemala.

This Venezuelan nicknamed "El Libertador" led armies that freed Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia from Spanish rule. He dreamed of a unified South America but saw it break apart. One country is named for him. For 10 points, name this leader.

This Indian leader used nonviolent civil disobedience, called satyagraha, to resist British rule. He was often called Mahatma, or "great soul." He was assassinated in New Delhi in January 1948. For 10 points, name this leader of the Indian independence movement.

In 1930, protesters led by Gandhi walked about 240 miles from Ahmedabad to the coastal village of Dandi. There he picked up a lump of natural salt in defiance of a British monopoly and tax. Thousands joined the nonviolent protest. For 10 points, name this campaign.

In 1868, a group of samurai and nobles restored the power of the emperor and ended the Tokugawa shogunate. The new government rapidly modernized Japan with railroads, a conscript army, and a constitution. For 10 points, name this transformation that took its name from an emperor.

This war began when Chinese official Lin Zexu destroyed chests of a drug seized from British merchants at Canton. Britain won, and the Treaty of Nanjing in 1842 gave it Hong Kong. For 10 points, name this war, fought over the trade in the drug from poppies.

The Society of Righteous and Harmonious Fists, called "Boxers" by Westerners, led this uprising against foreigners and Christians in China from 1899 to 1901. Rebels besieged foreign legations in Beijing until an eight-nation army relieved them. For 10 points, name this rebellion.

This man's Long March of 1934 to 1935 took Communist forces to Shaanxi province. He proclaimed the People's Republic of China in 1949. His Great Leap Forward and Cultural Revolution caused enormous suffering. For 10 points, name this Communist leader of China.

This doctor founded the Kuomintang and served as the first provisional president of the Republic of China in 1912. He promoted the "Three Principles of the People": nationalism, democracy, and livelihood. For 10 points, name this man regarded as the "father" of modern China.

From its capital at Istanbul, this empire at its height controlled the Balkans, the Middle East, and North Africa. Its elite infantry were called Janissaries, and its rulers bore the title sultan. It lasted until 1922. For 10 points, name this Turkish empire.

This sultan reigned from 1520 to 1566 and led armies to the gates of Vienna in 1529. He was known in Turkey as "the Lawgiver" and sponsored the architect Sinan. For 10 points, name this Ottoman ruler whose epithet is "the Magnificent."

In May 1453, this young Ottoman sultan captured Constantinople after a siege in which huge cannons broke the city walls. He converted the Hagia Sophia into a mosque. His victory ended the Byzantine Empire. For 10 points, name this sultan nicknamed "the Conqueror."

This Kurdish sultan of Egypt and Syria defeated Crusaders at the Battle of Hattin in 1187 and recaptured Jerusalem. He later fought Richard the Lionheart in the Third Crusade. For 10 points, name this Muslim leader.

Born in Mecca around 570, this man received revelations that were recorded in the Quran. In 622 he made the Hijra, or migration, to Medina. Muslims consider him the final prophet. For 10 points, name this founder of Islam.

Shah Jahan built this white marble tomb in Agra in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Construction took about twenty years and was completed around 1653. Its design combines Persian, Islamic, and Indian styles. For 10 points, name this monument.

This Mughal emperor ruled from 1556 to 1605 and was the grandson of Babur. He conquered much of northern India and married Hindu princesses. He built a new capital at Fatehpur Sikri and promoted religious tolerance. For 10 points, name this ruler.

This uprising began in 1857 in Meerut when Indian soldiers in the British East India Company's army refused to use rifle cartridges rumored to be greased with animal fat. It spread across northern India. Afterward, Britain ended Company rule and ruled India directly. For 10 points, name this revolt.

In August 1947, British India was divided into two independent countries, one largely Hindu and one largely Muslim. Millions of people crossed the new border, and hundreds of thousands were killed in violence. For 10 points, name this division of South Asia.

This South African activist spent 27 years in prison, mostly on Robben Island, for fighting apartheid. After his release in 1990, he shared the Nobel Peace Prize with F. W. de Klerk. In 1994 he became South Africa's first black president. For 10 points, name this man.

In 1948, South Africa's National Party formalized this system of racial segregation, whose name means "apartness" in Afrikaans. It forced people to live in separate areas and carry passes. It ended in the early 1990s. For 10 points, name this system of white minority rule.

This former enslaved man led the Haitian Revolution against French rule. He was captured by Napoleon's forces in 1802 and died in a French prison. His general Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared Haiti independent in 1804. For 10 points, name this Haitian leader.

This revolutionary overthrew Cuban dictator Fulgencio Batista in 1959. His government repelled the Bay of Pigs invasion in 1961 and allied with the Soviet Union. He ruled Cuba for decades. For 10 points, name this Cuban leader.

These warriors of feudal Japan followed a code of conduct called bushido. They served regional lords called daimyo and fought with swords called katana. The class was abolished after the Meiji Restoration. For 10 points, name this class of Japanese warriors.

In 1853, this American naval officer sailed four "black ships" into Edo Bay and demanded that Japan open to trade. The next year he signed the Treaty of Kanagawa. For 10 points, name this commodore who ended Japan's isolation.

This Zulu king built a powerful kingdom in southern Africa in the early 1800s. He introduced a short stabbing spear and reorganized his army into regiments. He was assassinated by his half-brothers in 1828. For 10 points, name this leader.

Opened in 1869 under the supervision of Ferdinand de Lesseps, this canal connected the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea. It shortened the sea route from Europe to Asia by avoiding the trip around Africa. For 10 points, name this Egyptian waterway.

Otto von Bismarck hosted this meeting of European powers in 1884 and 1885. Delegates set rules for dividing African territory among themselves. No African ruler was invited. For 10 points, name this conference that helped spark the "Scramble for Africa."

Between 1405 and 1433, this Chinese admiral commanded huge treasure fleets that sailed to India, Arabia, and East Africa. He served the Ming dynasty under the Yongle Emperor. For 10 points, name this eunuch and explorer.

q: In this novel, the title boy tricks his friends into whitewashing a fence for him and later witnesses a murder committed by Injun Joe. He is raised by his Aunt Polly in the town of Saint Petersburg and is sweet on Becky Thatcher. He and his friend Huck get lost in a cave and later find treasure. For 10 points, name this Mark Twain novel about a mischievous Missouri boy.

In this novel, a boy fakes his own death by killing a pig and splattering its blood in a cabin. The title character floats down a river with the escaped slave Jim, and meets two con men calling themselves the Duke and the King. He famously decides he will "go to hell" rather than turn Jim in. For 10 points, name this Mark Twain novel narrated by a boy raised by the Widow Douglas.

In this novel, Jess Aarons becomes friends with a new neighbor, Leslie Burke, after she beats the boys in a race. They build an imaginary kingdom in the woods across a creek, reached by swinging on a rope. Leslie dies when the rope breaks while Jess is away. For 10 points, name this Katherine Paterson novel about the kingdom of Terabithia.

The narrator of this novel, who asks to be called Ishmael, signs on to the whaling ship Pequod. The ship's captain has lost a leg and is obsessed with revenge, and the crew includes the harpooner Queequeg. It ends with a great white whale sinking the ship. For 10 points, name this novel by Herman Melville about Captain Ahab.

In this novel, Nick Carraway moves next door to a mysterious millionaire who throws lavish parties on Long Island. That millionaire stares at a green light at the end of a dock, hoping to win back Daisy Buchanan. It is set in the Jazz Age. For 10 points, name this F. Scott Fitzgerald novel about Jay Gatsby.

In this novel, a lawyer defends Tom Robinson, a Black man falsely accused of assault, in the town of Maycomb, Alabama. The story is narrated by his young daughter Scout, and her brother Jem. The reclusive Boo Radley saves the children from an attack. For 10 points, name this novel by Harper Lee.

In this novella, two migrant workers named George and Lennie dream of owning a farm where they can raise rabbits. Lennie, a gentle but very strong man, accidentally kills the wife of Curley. George makes a terrible decision beside a river at the end. For 10 points, name this short novel by John Steinbeck.

The narrator of this novel is expelled from Pencey Prep and wanders around New York City. He thinks most people are "phonies" and wants to protect children from falling off a cliff while playing in a field of rye. He has a sister named Phoebe. For 10 points, name this J. D. Salinger novel about Holden Caulfield.

In this novel, a Saint Bernard and Scottish shepherd mix named Buck is stolen from a California ranch and sold to be a sled dog. He joins the Klondike Gold Rush and eventually answers the call of his wolf ancestors. For 10 points, name this Jack London novel set in the Yukon.

This novel follows four sisters named Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy March, who grow up in Massachusetts while their father serves in the Civil War. Jo is an aspiring writer who cuts off her hair, and Beth dies of scarlet fever. For 10 points, name this novel by Louisa May Alcott.

The narrator of this novel is a greaser named Ponyboy Curtis, whose brother Darry looks after him after their parents die. After Johnny kills a Soc named Bob, Johnny and Ponyboy hide in an abandoned church. The poem "Nothing Gold Can Stay" is quoted in it. For 10 points, name this S. E. Hinton novel.

In this poem, a narrator mourns his lost Lenore while a visitor taps at his chamber door. A bird perched on a bust of Pallas says only one word in response to his questions. That word is "nevermore." For 10 points, name this poem by Edgar Allan Poe.

This poet wrote of a traveler who "took the one less traveled by" at a fork in a yellow wood. He also wrote "Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening" and "Fire and Ice." He recited a poem at John F. Kennedy's inauguration. For 10 points, name this New England poet of "The Road Not Taken."

This poet's collection Leaves of Grass included "Song of Myself" and was revised throughout his life. He wrote "O Captain! My Captain!" about the death of Abraham Lincoln. He worked as a nurse in the Civil War. For 10 points, name this American poet who celebrated himself and sang the body electric.

This poet of Amherst, Massachusetts wrote "Because I could not stop for Death" and "Hope is the thing with feathers." She rarely published during her life and used many dashes in her poems. Almost 1,800 of her poems were found after she died. For 10 points, name this reclusive poet.
